title: Why These Subjects?
author: Jo Fujiwara
summary: Fujiwara investigates why nearly every school system in the world, regardless of language or culture, converges on the same core subjects -- mathematics, language, science, and history -- despite those systems developing largely independently across civilizations. Surveying examination systems in imperial China, Tokugawa Japan, South Asia, and the Islamic world, he argues the convergence is not proof of one universal discovery but evidence that societies repeatedly encounter the same educational problems, later reinforced by the twentieth-century spread of a standardized nation-state schooling model documented by comparative-education researcher Aaron Benavot. Fujiwara contends these subjects persist because they function as 'powerful knowledge' -- content that helps students organize and evaluate other knowledge, not because they are traditional or sacred. He examines two cautionary case studies, Japan's early-2000s 'relaxed education' reform and Finland's widely misreported 'abolition of subjects,' to argue that cutting core content and time carries real costs, while claims that Finland eliminated subjects were factually wrong. He closes by arguing that AI raises the stakes for this foundation rather than lowering them, since a mind that holds a coherent knowledge map is the only thing capable of noticing when an AI's polished answer is wrong.
points: Independent examination traditions in China, Korea, Japan, South Asia, and the Islamic world converged on similar subject categories not through isolated discovery but through centuries of borrowing, adaptation, and shared practical problems.

Aaron Benavot's comparative study of primary curricula worldwide from 1920-1986 found subject categories converged across rich and poor countries alike, driven by the spread of a standardized 'modern nation-state school' model rather than economic development.

Japan's 2002 'relaxed education' reform (yutori kyoiku) preceded a measurable decline in Japan's PISA rankings -- the 'PISA shock' -- though Fujiwara cautions the causal story is more complicated than the headlines suggested.

Finland's widely cited 'abolition of school subjects' was misreported: the 2014 curriculum kept subject teaching intact and simply added required multidisciplinary modules assessed against each subject's own objectives.
Fujiwara's closing argument: AI makes disciplinary knowledge more valuable, not less, because a mind that holds a map can challenge the route it is handed -- but only if it has a map to begin with.
quotes: My answer is not that everyone independently discovered the same canon, but the same educational problems seem to reappear in education.

Aaron Benavot and colleagues, experts in comparative studies in education, examined official primary curricula worldwide from 1920 to 1986. Across very disparate countries, rich and poor, the subject categories and the shares of the week given to them converged.

Language, mathematics, science, and history do unusually generative work because knowledge in each helps a student acquire and judge knowledge elsewhere, as well as helps to organize a larger body of knowledge and skills.

It was not true. The curriculum kept subject teaching and required each school to run at least one multidisciplinary learning module a year, with assessment inside those modules still tied to the objectives of the participating subjects.

AI makes the value of this knowledge more visible and less likely to be attained. It can produce a polished answer that is incomplete or wrong. Knowledge helps users notice errors, question conclusions, and check sources.
A school that answers a biased canon by teaching less has only ensured that fewer children have anything to argue with.
